paras: The theft of a Black Pullman passenger's shoes near Cairo, Illinois, was an undated incident in which several white passengers on a train from Chicago threw a Black man's shoes out of the window overnight, leaving him to leave the train at Cairo in his socks. It is known only from a white Jackson, Mississippi, columnist's own recollection, told as a joke and reprinted by the New York Age on June 21, 1919.

The story appeared as an aside in a Jackson Clarion Ledger column on Illinois becoming the first state legislature to ratify the woman suffrage amendment. The writer complained that Illinois "does not draw the color line in the least" and that Black travelers could ride in coaches and Pullmans if they could pay. That point, he wrote, recalled "a little incident in the life of the writer" on a trip home from Chicago, for which he gave no date.

According to the columnist, a Black man in one of the Pullman sections was "taking all the privileges the Pullman afforded," and several white men "grew tired of him" and planned to "take him down a peg or two." During a bitterly cold night they stole his shoes and threw them out of the window. When the train reached Cairo about daybreak, the man protested to the porter, swore, and threatened to sue the company for damages. He was nonetheless put off at Cairo and was last seen walking through the snow in his socks while, the writer said, the passengers laughed.
The column names neither the passenger nor the men involved, and no report of a complaint, suit, or arrest was found.

The only coverage found was the New York Age's reprint of the column under the heading "A Mississippi View." The original writer framed the episode as comedy, describing the passenger with racial slurs and closing with the line that he was "making foot-prints in the sands of time." The Age printed the column in full, slurs included, without comment in the text of the reprint.

reader.title: Theft of a Black Pullman passenger's shoes near Cairo, Illinois
bases: Several white passengers stole a Black passenger's shoes and threw them from the train, a prank-style harassment involving property and no violence to the person, told as an undated personal recollection rather than reported as news (A1).
The only account is a white Mississippi columnist's own recollection, reprinted once in the New York Age (A1); no other report was found.

accounts.label: White columnist's recollection
accounts.gist: A Jackson Clarion Ledger writer, reprinted in the New York Age, said several white Pullman passengers threw a Black man's shoes out of the window to 'take him down a peg or two', and that the passengers laughed as he walked through the snow at Cairo in his socks.

framing.detail: The New York Age reprinted the Mississippi column verbatim under 'A Mississippi View', including the white writer's mocking anecdote and slurs, without inline comment.

record_check.dossier: other: a prank-style theft of a passenger's shoes by several white passengers, with no assault on the person and no mob
Undated past incident recalled in a column reprinted 1919-06-21; not a 1919 event as far as the text shows
Aboard a train from Chicago; Cairo is where the passenger was put off, not necessarily where the shoes were thrown out
One unnamed Black male Pullman passenger
The men 'grew tired of him' for 'taking all the privileges the Pullman afforded' and wanted to 'take him down a peg or two'

info: Undated; the writer recalls it as a past 'little incident' on a winter night trip home from Chicago ('bitter cold', snow).
On a Pullman car of a train returning from Chicago; the train reached Cairo about daybreak, where the passenger was put off.
One unnamed Black man traveling in a Pullman section, described by the writer in derogatory terms.
None; the writer says the white men 'grew tired of him' because he was 'taking all the privileges the Pullman afforded'.
Several white men among the Pullman passengers; the writer was present and does not say whether he took part.
No report of any suit, complaint, or arrest was found.

sources.note: Reprint, under 'A Mississippi View', of a Jackson Clarion Ledger column on Illinois suffrage in which the white writer recalls, as a joke, white Pullman passengers throwing a Black man's shoes off the train before Cairo; undated, victim unnamed.
quotes: Several white men grew tired of him, and concocted a plan to take him down a peg or two.
They decided to steal the Negro's shoes during the night, which was bitter cold, and throw them out of the window.
This reference to Negroes riding in Pullman recalls a little incident in the life of the writer.
He was compelled to get off at Cairo and the last seen of him he was making tracks through the snow in his sock-foot, to the nearest social-equality hotel
